text: Animal movement control is an important part of disease prevention for smallholder farms because an apparently healthy animal can carry infection before signs appear. Farmers should know the source of purchased animals whenever possible, avoid buying visibly sick animals, and keep simple records of purchases, sales, movements, and vaccination history. Newly purchased or returning animals (including those that went to a market and came back unsold) should ideally be kept separate from established animals and observed before introduction, with the isolation period set by disease risk and veterinary guidance rather than a universal number. Livestock markets create real transmission risk because animals from many farms mix in one place. During the wet season (roughly May–October), muddy roads and wet equipment complicate hygiene and transport; during the dry season (roughly November–April), dust, heat stress, and animal movement around water sources create additional challenges. Vehicles, cages, footwear, and equipment can carry pathogens between farms even without a visibly sick animal moving. Sick animals should never be taken to a market for sale. If a serious contagious disease is suspected, unnecessary animal movement and sales should stop while veterinary or official guidance is obtained — this applies particularly to foot-and-mouth disease and African swine fever. No breed or variety is assigned to Preah Vihear from location alone; the actual animal type and source should be recorded rather than guessed.
